findings.title: Denial cache entries are never invalidated, so previously-denied resources stay denied for up to 30s after a permission grant
findings.body: After a Check returns Allowed=false, the code calls s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). Nothing in this PR (or anywhere else visible in the diff) ever calls Delete on permDenialCache, so entries only expire via the 30-second TTL. Once a (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple has been denied, the user will keep receiving Allowed=false on that exact tuple for up to 30 seconds — even after a permission grant (role assignment, dashboard share, etc.) makes them eligible. This is a regression relative to the pre-PR flow, where a re-check after a grant would consult the DB and return the updated permission; the new denial cache short-circuits that re-check. As a consequence, the same user with the same role can see inconsistent behavior: a brand-new dashboard they have never asked about returns Allowed=true (no prior denial entry), while a dashboard they queried once before the grant returns Allowed=false until the entry expires. The denial cache should be invalidated (e.g., on role/permission changes or dashboard creation/sharing) so grants take effect promptly.

findings.title: Denial cache key uses raw userUID while permission cache uses the resolved UID
findings.body: The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the request subject by validateSubject. The permission cache key in getCachedIdentityPermissions is built from userIdentifiers.UID, the value returned by GetUserIdentifiers. GetUserIdentifiers treats a purely-numeric userUID as a user ID and resolves it to the user's canonical UID (typically a non-numeric string). For the same user, denial cache entries therefore live under one identifier and permission cache entries under another, so the two caches never share state. Concretely, if a user is identified by numeric ID '123' the denial cache is keyed by '123', while the permission cache is keyed by the resolved UID (e.g., 'abc456'); a denial cached under '123' will never block a request that arrives with subject 'user:abc456' (and vice versa). The denial cache key should be built from the same resolved UID that the permission cache uses.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits
findings.body: When the denial cache hits, Check increments permissionCacheUsage with label value 'true'. The same metric and label are used later for genuine permission-cache hits (line 132). The 'true' label therefore no longer means 'permission cache hit' — it means 'either permission cache or denial cache hit'. Existing dashboards/alerts built on this metric will silently change meaning after this PR. The denial cache hit should be recorded under a distinct metric name or a distinct label (e.g., cache='denial' vs cache='permission').

findings.title: No regression test for a stale denial cache entry after a permission grant
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck covers a denial cache hit that has just been written (subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry'), but it does not cover the regression scenario where a denial cache entry sits for the full 30-second window while the underlying permission is granted (e.g., via role assignment or dashboard share). Given that permDenialCache has no invalidation path anywhere in the change, a test should pin down what happens when a previously-denied Check is re-run after the DB now grants the permission; with the current code the response is still Allowed=false for up to 30 seconds, and there is no test that would catch the resulting regression.

findings.title: Test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' uses a scope value of false but its comment claims it allows access
findings.body: The new subtest primes permCache with map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} and the inline comment says this 'allow[s] access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope map entry with value false does not represent a granted scope — the map is effectively empty for the requested resource, so it does not actually demonstrate the intended precedence (denial cache over an allowed scope). To demonstrate that the denial cache takes precedence over a granted scope, the entry should be set to true (map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': true}); otherwise the test would pass even if the permCache lookup was silently dropped from the Check path.
